ideas.title: Psychometric Analysis of Multimodal Safety: IRT for Vision-Language Safety Benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# Psychometric Analysis of Multimodal Safety: IRT for Vision-Language Safety Benchmarks

**Problem:** All IRT applications to AI evaluation use text-only benchmarks. Multimodal models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini) are evaluated on vision-language safety benchmarks (e.g., MMSafetyBench, FigStep), but the psychometric properties of these benchmarks are unknown. Research shows MMMU and MathVista exhibit less than 5% performance gaps between multimodal and text-only models — suggesting many 'multimodal' benchmarks aren't measuring visual input. IRT can empirically test whether vision adds discriminative information.

**Direction:** Collect binary response matrices from public multimodal safety benchmarks for 15-20 models. Fit a unidimensional IRT model and examine: (1) whether vision-specific items show systematically different discrimination parameters than text-only items on the same benchmark, (2) whether residuals from a text-ability factor are correlated with vision-specific features (using a MIRT model with a vision-specific residual factor), (3) whether IRT item information peaks at different ability levels for visual vs. text safety items.

**Why it matters:** If visual safety items show no psychometric differentiation from text safety items (same discrimination, same difficulty ordering), this is empirical evidence that multimodal safety benchmarks are not measuring vision at all — they measure text-based safety with image distractors. This would be a major validity critique of the multimodal safety evaluation field.

**Relevant context:** MMSafetyBench, VLSafe, and FigStep are public multimodal safety benchmarks. Research (2024-2025) found many multimodal benchmarks fail to require visual processing. IRT can detect this through dimensionality testing. The mirt package handles this analysis. This would be the first psychometric analysis of multimodal safety benchmarks.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: if multimodal safety benchmarks don't actually measure visual safety, the field has a false sense of multimodal safety coverage. Gap: revealing the problem doesn't directly reduce risk.

low_compute.reasoning: IRT analysis in R on existing data. CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Standard IRT plus MIRT analysis. Intermediate. Requires understanding of multimodal benchmark design.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused: fit IRT to multimodal safety benchmark, compare visual vs text item parameters. Requires obtaining multimodal benchmark response matrices.

**Direction:** Fit a multidimensional IRT model to a multi-domain safety benchmark, generating test information functions and ability profiles per safety dimension, identifying where on the safety ability continuum each model's measurement is most uncertain.

**Why it matters:** Multidimensional IRT (MIRT) produces separate ability estimates per latent dimension, giving diagnostic profiles rather than aggregate scores. Information functions reveal which ability ranges are well-measured for each safety dimension. This directly provides the per-dimension weakness diagnosis that aggregate scores cannot.

**Relevant context:** The mirt R package supports full multidimensional IRT analysis. MetaBench (ICLR 2025) applies IRT across multiple benchmark dimensions. original_idea.body:
# IRT-Based Formal Power Analysis for Safety Benchmark Design

**Problem:** No published AI safety benchmark was designed with a formal power analysis specifying the minimum number of items required to reliably distinguish models at a given safety ability difference. Item counts are chosen arbitrarily. IRT power analysis methods (e.g., detecting a 0.5 theta difference between models with 80% power) have never been applied to AI safety benchmark design.

**Direction:** Use the mirt R package and its simulate functions to conduct Monte Carlo IRT power analyses for representative safety benchmark scenarios. Vary: number of items (20, 50, 100, 200), item discrimination (a=0.5 to 2.0), ability difference to detect (0.3, 0.5, 1.0 theta units), and item pool difficulty distribution. Report power curves and minimum item counts for each scenario. Apply results to critique the item counts of 3-4 existing safety benchmarks. Derive practical sample-size guidelines for future benchmark designers.

**Why it matters:** Without power analysis, safety benchmark designers cannot know whether their benchmark has sufficient statistical power to distinguish models of interest. This is the direct AI safety analogue of open problem 11 (no IRT power analysis for AI). Results would provide the first principled item-count recommendations for safety benchmarks, with immediate practical utility for AISI, METR, and similar organizations.

**Relevant context:** Open problem 11 from MTAI framework (no formal IRT power analysis for AI); mirt R package simulation capabilities; sample size analysis for ML validation (PMC 2023); N-Power AI framework (bioRxiv 2025); tinyBenchmarks finding that 100 items from 14K MMLU suffice.

Names the specific mechanism but the chain to catastrophic risk reduction has a gap -- it produces design guidelines rather than directly detecting risk.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Monte Carlo simulation in mirt follows documented patterns. The student needs to understand IRT parameters and power analysis concepts, but the simulation framework is well-structured. A mentor could set up the simulation template.

narrow_scope.reasoning: A single simulation study with well-defined parameter grid. The first deliverable (power curves for one scenario) is tightly scoped and self-contained. Extensions to multiple benchmarks are natural add-ons.

# tinyBenchmarks Failure Modes: When Does IRT-Based Item Selection Break Under Distribution Shift?

**Problem:** tinyBenchmarks (Polo et al. 2024) showed 100 IRT-selected MMLU items suffice to estimate full-benchmark performance (correlation ~0.99). The authors note IRT-based anchors are 'only slightly affected' by distribution shift, but 'slightly' is unquantified. We do not know the conditions under which estimation error becomes practically unacceptable.

**Direction:** Using the public tinyBenchmarks data and Open LLM Leaderboard scores, systematically simulate distribution shift: hold out model subgroups (e.g., only instruction-tuned models, only models <7B, only code-specialised models) from the calibration set and measure estimation error on the held-out group. Plot RMSE and rank-correlation as a function of how different the held-out group is from calibration. Identify the threshold at which the 100-item estimate degrades beyond a pre-specified tolerance (e.g., >5 rank positions).

**Why it matters:** Safety evaluators who adopt sparse benchmarks need to know when those benchmarks fail. If IRT-CAT degrades for novel model architectures, early-warning safety evaluations of frontier models may be systematically miscalibrated.

**Relevant context:** tinyBenchmarks (arXiv 2402.14992); tinyMMLU dataset on HuggingFace; IRT calibration in R (mirt package); Open LLM Leaderboard for model metadata.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: if sparse benchmarks fail for novel architectures, safety evaluations of frontier models may be miscalibrated. Names the specific mechanism (distribution shift in IRT calibration) but this is about evaluation robustness rather than directly targeting a risk pathway.

low_compute.reasoning: Uses existing tinyBenchmarks data and leaderboard scores. IRT fitting in R, no model inference.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires understanding IRT calibration, distribution shift concepts, and systematic simulation design. The hold-out methodology is standard ML practice which CS students know, adapted to IRT context.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped single experiment: take tinyBenchmarks items, hold out model subgroups, measure estimation error. First deliverable is a plot of RMSE vs. held-out group characteristics.

# Automated Test Assembly (ATA) Optimization for Efficient Safety Benchmark Design

**Problem:** Safety benchmarks are assembled heuristically—researchers add items that seem useful until the set is 'large enough.' Automated test assembly from educational measurement optimally selects items from an item bank to maximize measurement precision for a target ability range while satisfying content constraints (blueprint coverage, format balance, item exposure limits).

**Direction:** Adapt ATA methodology: using calibrated item parameters from existing IRT analyses of safety benchmarks (already available from arXiv 2505.15055 and related work), formulate the benchmark assembly problem as an integer programming problem. Minimize benchmark length while (a) achieving target measurement precision at the critical safety threshold, (b) satisfying content blueprint constraints, and (c) limiting item exposure. Use R (lpSolve or ompr package) to solve. Show what a psychometrically optimized 50-item safety benchmark would look like vs. the current 500-item benchmark.

**Why it matters:** ATA can produce shorter, more precise benchmarks that are less susceptible to gaming and less expensive to run—critical advantages as evaluation costs scale with model size. Showing a benchmark can be 10x shorter with equivalent precision would fundamentally change evaluation economics.

**Relevant context:** ATA is a mature educational measurement technique (test assembly constraint programming literature). Recent CAT paper (arXiv 2603.23506) shows 1.3% of items achieve near-perfect correlation in adaptive testing. R lpSolve/ompr packages support integer programming. Calibrated item parameters already available for major benchmarks. Requires no new data collection.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: more efficient benchmarks lower evaluation costs, enabling broader adoption of safety testing. The mechanism is clear but indirect -- efficiency is an enabler, not a direct safety intervention.

low_compute.reasoning: Integer programming in R using pre-existing IRT parameters. No model inference needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires understanding both IRT information functions and integer programming (lpSolve). Formulating the optimization problem with constraints requires some mathematical maturity. However, the lpSolve package handles the solving.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-scoped: take existing item parameters, define constraints, run optimization, report the optimized item set. Clear single deliverable comparing optimized vs. original benchmark.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses safety benchmark efficiency using ATA with IRT parameters; safety relevance is clear for producing shorter, more precise safety evaluations.

ideas.title: Adaptive Safety Probing: Simulating CAT Administration of Safety Items

original_idea.body:
# Adaptive Safety Probing: Simulating CAT Administration of Safety Items

**Problem:** Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT) efficiently estimates ability using far fewer items by selecting items based on current ability estimates. Medical CAT achieves r=0.988 with 1.3% of items. Safety evaluations currently administer fixed item banks exhaustively. A CAT simulation could identify the minimum number of items needed for reliable safety ability estimation.

**Direction:** Using item parameters from a 2PL IRT model fitted to a safety benchmark (mirt R), simulate CAT administration using the catR package. Use maximum information item selection and various stopping rules (SE < 0.3, minimum 10 items). Compare: final theta estimates from CAT vs. full-test administration; number of items required by CAT; which items are most frequently selected (revealing which items are most informative for safety ability estimation). Report the reduction in items achievable with r > 0.95 recovery.

**Why it matters:** If safety evaluations can be reduced from 500 items to 50 items with minimal loss of precision using CAT principles, evaluation cost and time drops by 90%—making comprehensive safety evaluation far more tractable for smaller labs and regulators. The cold-start problem (open problem 4) means operational CAT is not yet feasible, but simulations demonstrate the theoretical efficiency ceiling and identify highest-information safety items.

**Relevant context:** Medical CAT: r=0.988 with 1.3% of items (Paper cited in topic context); tinyBenchmarks: 100 items from 14K MMLU with 1.9% error; catR R package for CAT simulation; open problem 4 (cold-start for adaptive approaches); mirt IRT calibration as prerequisite.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: more efficient safety evaluation means more labs can afford to evaluate, increasing safety coverage. The mechanism is clear but indirect -- efficiency gains are valuable but do not directly address a specific risk pathway.

low_compute.reasoning: CAT simulation in R using pre-calibrated item parameters. No model inference needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires understanding both IRT calibration (prerequisite) and CAT simulation (catR package). The catR package provides high-level functions but understanding stopping rules and item selection requires IRT background. Two-step pipeline adds complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear first deliverable: run CAT simulation on one benchmark, report items needed vs. correlation with full test. The catR package makes this a well-defined single experiment.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses safety evaluation efficiency with a concrete CAT simulation approach; safety relevance is clear for making safety evaluation more tractable.

ideas.title: Bookmark Method for Proficiency Level Classification on Safety Benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# Bookmark Method for Proficiency Level Classification on Safety Benchmarks

**Problem:** Safety evaluations rarely distinguish between 'dangerous,' 'borderline,' and 'safe' models with more than one binary threshold. Ordinal proficiency classification (e.g., unsafe / marginal / safe / exemplary) would provide richer information for governance decisions but no methodology exists for setting multiple cutscores.

**Direction:** Apply the Bookmark standard-setting method: arrange benchmark items in order of IRT-estimated difficulty (already done in recent LLM-IRT papers), present this ordered 'item booklet' to safety expert panelists, and ask them to place bookmarks at the transitions between proficiency levels. Run three iterative rounds with feedback. This yields multiple, data-driven thresholds on the same scale. Implement in R using existing IRT packages (mirt, ltm) on open leaderboard data.

**Why it matters:** Ordinal classification enables risk-tiered governance: models in the 'marginal' band get additional scrutiny, 'unsafe' models are barred, and 'exemplary' models receive deployment fast-tracks. The Bookmark method is more tractable than Angoff for large item pools and produces thresholds anchored to item difficulty statistics.

**Relevant context:** Bookmark method literature establishes three iterative rounds with norming data as standard procedure. Recent LLM-IRT papers (arXiv 2505.15055, Stanford CRFM 2025) have already estimated item difficulty parameters for major benchmarks, providing the raw material for bookmark placement without additional coding.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: principled safety thresholds enable risk-tiered governance, directly determining which models can be deployed. Every link is explicit: IRT difficulty ordering -> expert bookmark placement -> proficiency levels -> governance decisions. Targets a critical gap in safety governance.

low_compute.reasoning: Uses pre-existing IRT parameters from published papers. The Bookmark method itself is a human panel exercise, not computational.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: The IRT part uses existing results. However, the Bookmark method requires recruiting and coordinating safety expert panelists for three iterative rounds, which is a logistical challenge. The methodology itself is straightforward but the human coordination is non-trivial for students.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires recruiting expert panelists and running three rounds of bookmark placement. The three-round panel process is substantial. A minimal version with one round and 2-3 panelists could be a first deliverable, but standard methodology requires three rounds.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined AI safety problem (setting meaningful safety thresholds) with a clear Bookmark standard-setting methodology using IRT-calibrated items; scope is precise and directly governance-relevant.

ideas.title: Angoff Standard-Setting for AI Safety Cutoffs

original_idea.body:
# Angoff Standard-Setting for AI Safety Cutoffs: Using Expert Panels to Define Meaningful Pass/Fail Thresholds on Safety Benchmarks

**Problem:** AI safety benchmarks currently use arbitrary numeric cutoffs (e.g., 80% refusal rate = 'safe') with no principled justification for why those thresholds represent meaningful safety distinctions. There is no structured method for translating benchmark scores into defensible deployment decisions.

**Direction:** Convene a structured Angoff panel of AI safety researchers who each estimate, item by item on an existing safety benchmark (e.g., MLCommons AI Safety v0.5 or StrongREJECT), the probability that a 'minimally safe' model would answer correctly. Average these estimates across panelists to derive a principled cutoff score. Analyze inter-panelist agreement (intraclass correlation), compare the resulting threshold to current ad hoc cutoffs, and examine whether the Angoff-derived cutoff changes deployment recommendations for existing model evaluations. Run the exercise with two panels (safety researchers vs. AI ethicists) and compare results as a convergent validity check.

**Why it matters:** Without principled standard-setting, AI safety thresholds are arbitrary and legally/ethically indefensible. Angoff panels have been used for decades in high-stakes credentialing (medical licensing, bar exams) to produce defensible cutoffs. Importing this methodology would make AI safety thresholds transparent, reproducible, and grounded in expert judgment rather than convention.

**Relevant context:** The MLCommons AI Safety Benchmark v0.5 explicitly acknowledges that determining cutoffs is an open problem. The contrasting groups and Angoff methods are both well-validated in clinical skills assessment literature (PMC12409087). Educational measurement R tools (eatATA, mirt) support the analysis. No prior work appears to have used structured standard-setting methodology for AI safety benchmark thresholds.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: arbitrary safety thresholds undermine regulatory and deployment decisions, and principled Angoff-derived cutoffs directly address this. Every link is explicit: arbitrary threshold -> meaningless pass/fail -> unsafe deployments. Principled thresholds are immediately actionable.

low_compute.reasoning: No compute needed. The method is expert panel judgment, statistical analysis of agreement (ICC), and comparison of thresholds. CPU-only R analysis.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: The Angoff method itself is conceptually simple (experts estimate probabilities). Organizing panels and computing ICC is intermediate. The main challenge is recruiting panelists, not technical complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires recruiting expert panels, running the Angoff exercise, and computing agreement statistics. The logistics of panel recruitment make this a sustained effort, though a single-panel exercise on one benchmark is feasible.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined AI safety governance problem (principled deployment thresholds) with clear Angoff methodology; safety relevance is obvious and directly actionable for regulators.

ideas.title: Score Equating for AI Safety Benchmarks: Enabling Fair Cross-Benchmark Comparison

original_idea.body:
# Score Equating for AI Safety Benchmarks: Enabling Fair Cross-Benchmark Comparison Using Equipercentile Linking

**Problem:** Different AI safety benchmarks (e.g., StrongREJECT vs. MLCommons vs. SORRY-Bench) are not on a common scale, making it impossible to meaningfully compare models evaluated on different benchmarks. A model scoring 85% on one benchmark may be safer or less safe than a model scoring 70% on another—with no principled way to compare.

**Direction:** Select two or more safety benchmarks that have been administered to a common set of models. Using those models as the 'linking sample,' apply equipercentile equating (or IRT-based observed-score equating) to place both benchmarks on a common scale. Use the equate R package. Evaluate linking quality using the standard error of equating and the degree of model rank-order change post-equating. Produce a concordance table allowing practitioners to convert scores across benchmarks. Validate by checking whether equated scores predict human-judged safety ratings better than raw scores.

**Why it matters:** Score equating is the foundational method for making test scores comparable across forms in education (SAT, GRE) and medicine. Without it, comparing models evaluated on different benchmarks is like comparing Fahrenheit and Celsius without a conversion formula. The equate R package implements all standard equating methods without heavy coding. This could immediately improve how AI labs, regulators, and researchers compare safety claims.

**Relevant context:** The 'Psychometrically derived 60-question benchmarks' paper (ScienceDirect 2025) shows IRT-based cross-benchmark work is feasible. The equate R package is mature and widely used. Several safety benchmarks have been run on overlapping model sets (e.g., Llama family, GPT-4 class). Score equating has been discussed conceptually in AI evaluation literature but empirical equating studies appear absent from the literature.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: incomparable benchmark scores lead to misleading cross-benchmark safety claims. The risk mechanism is named but the chain has a gap: equating improves comparability but the safety impact depends on whether cross-benchmark comparison drives actual deployment decisions.

low_compute.reasoning: Equipercentile equating in R on existing score data. Minimal compute, CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: The equate R package handles the heavy lifting. Understanding equating concepts and interpreting results requires intermediate statistical knowledge. Finding overlapping model sets across benchmarks requires some data work.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: equate two benchmarks using a common model set, produce a concordance table. A single well-defined analysis with a concrete, useful output.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses cross-benchmark comparability for safety evaluation with concrete equipercentile equating; safety relevance is clear for regulatory comparisons.

ideas.title: Adaptive Safety Testing via IRT-Based Item Selection: Designing a CAT Safety Benchmark

original_idea.body:
# Adaptive Safety Testing via IRT-Based Item Selection: Designing a Computerized Adaptive Safety Benchmark That Converges in Fewer Items

**Problem:** Current safety benchmarks administer the same fixed set of hundreds of items to every model regardless of its safety level, making evaluation slow and expensive. A model that fails basic safety items should not waste evaluation time on advanced items, and vice versa. This is the unsolved problem that CAT has addressed in education for 40 years.

**Direction:** Using publicly available response data from a safety benchmark with many items (e.g., WildGuard, SORRY-Bench, or HarmBench), fit an IRT model (2PL or Rasch) to estimate item difficulty and discrimination parameters. Simulate a CAT algorithm using the mirtCAT R package: start with moderate-difficulty items, select next items based on maximum information at the current ability estimate, stop when SE falls below a threshold. Compare the number of items needed to achieve equivalent measurement precision versus fixed-form administration. Evaluate convergence speed and rank-order fidelity for the CAT vs. full benchmark.

**Why it matters:** The recent paper 'Leveraging CAT for Cost-effective Evaluation of LLMs in Medical Benchmarking' (arxiv 2603.23506) shows CAT achieves near-perfect correlation with full-bank estimates using only 1.3% of items in medical benchmarks. The CAT4AI framework already exists on GitHub. Applying this specifically to safety benchmarks could reduce evaluation cost by 90%+ while maintaining precision. mirtCAT in R makes simulation straightforward without ML training.

**Relevant context:** CAT has been applied to AI benchmarks in medical contexts (arxiv 2603.23506) and via the CAT4AI Python library (GitHub bigdata-ustc). The 'From Static Benchmarks to Adaptive Testing' paper (arxiv 2306.10512) explicitly proposes this direction for AI evaluation. mirtCAT and catR are R packages supporting CAT simulation. Safety benchmarks like SORRY-Bench have 400+ items—sufficient for IRT calibration. This application specifically to safety benchmarks with analysis of item-type coverage appears novel.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: expensive evaluation reduces evaluation frequency, and CAT makes it cheaper. But the impact on catastrophic risk is indirect: cheaper evaluation enables more frequent evaluation, which may catch more issues. The chain has a gap between efficiency and safety improvement.

low_compute.reasoning: CAT simulation in R on existing response data. Minimal compute, CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: mirtCAT package handles the CAT simulation. Understanding IRT calibration and CAT logic requires intermediate psychometric knowledge but is well-supported by package documentation.

ideas.title: Bookmark Method Standard Setting for AI Safety Benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# Bookmark Method Standard Setting for AI Safety Benchmarks: Using Ordered Item Booklet Methodology to Set Defensible Performance Level Descriptors

**Problem:** AI safety benchmarks lack formal Performance Level Descriptors (PLDs)—descriptions of what a model at each safety level actually does and does not do. Without PLDs, safety grades (e.g., 'Low Risk,' 'High Risk') are labels without behavioral content. The Bookmark method provides a structured procedure for deriving PLDs from expert judgment about item difficulty ordering.

**Direction:** Implement the Bookmark method for a safety benchmark: (1) Order items by their IRT-estimated difficulty (probability that a model of any given safety level answers correctly). (2) Create an Ordered Item Booklet (OIB) presenting items from easiest to hardest. (3) Have a panel of AI safety experts 'bookmark' the location where the transition from one performance level to the next occurs. (4) Average bookmarks across panelists to set the cutoff. (5) Develop PLDs describing what models at each level do. (6) Compare Bookmark-derived cutoffs to Angoff-derived cutoffs and current ad hoc thresholds.

**Why it matters:** The Bookmark method is the most widely used alternative to Angoff for high-stakes standard setting and has shown superior validity in medical education (BMC Medical Education 2020). It produces not just cutoffs but interpretable descriptions of what each performance level means—critical for regulatory communication. An OIB requires IRT difficulty estimates plus expert judgment, with no heavy coding required.

**Relevant context:** Bookmark vs. Angoff comparison studies show Bookmark produces higher validity indices (BMC Medical Education 2020). The Bookmark method is used for NAEP, ACCUPLACER, and other high-stakes assessments. R packages for IRT difficulty estimation (eRm, mirt, TAM) provide the necessary inputs. AI safety benchmarks lack formal PLDs that could guide deployment decisions. No published work applies Bookmark methodology to AI safety evaluation.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: lack of PLDs means safety grades are labels without behavioral content, undermining deployment decisions. Bookmark-derived PLDs make safety levels interpretable, directly improving regulatory communication and deployment decisions.

low_compute.reasoning: IRT difficulty estimation in R plus expert panel judgment. Minimal compute, CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: The Bookmark method is conceptually accessible (order items, have experts place bookmarks). IRT calibration for difficulty ordering is intermediate. Panel logistics add non-technical complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires IRT calibration, creating ordered item booklet, recruiting and running expert panel, and developing PLDs. Panel logistics make this a sustained multi-week effort even for one benchmark.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined AI safety governance problem (setting defensible performance level descriptors) with clear Bookmark methodology using IRT; scope is precise and directly actionable.

# IRT-Based Adaptive Item Selection for Safety Evaluation: Does It Preserve Ranking Accuracy?

**Problem:** Apply IRT to AI safety benchmarks

**Direction:** Using pre-calibrated IRT parameters from a safety benchmark, simulate a computerized adaptive testing (CAT) procedure in R: starting with items of medium difficulty, adaptively select next items based on maximum Fisher information at the current theta estimate, and stop when standard error falls below 0.3. Compare safety ability estimates from CAT (using ~20% of items) against full-benchmark estimates and measure rank-order correlation between models.

**Why it matters:** Safety evaluations are expensive—running hundreds of models across thousands of items consumes significant compute. If IRT-based adaptive selection can accurately rank models using 10-20% of items, this would drastically reduce evaluation costs while maintaining the same discriminative validity. Recent work achieved 98%+ cost reduction for medical benchmarks using this approach.

**Relevant context:** CAT for LLM evaluation has been validated for medical benchmarks (2026 preprint): CAT-derived proficiency estimates achieved near-perfect correlation with full-bank estimates using only 1.3% of items. The tinyBenchmarks paper (2024) showed 160x cost reduction on Open LLM Leaderboard using IRT item selection. Safety benchmarks are a natural next target.

# Standard-Setting Study: What Evaluation Score Should Constitute a Safety Pass/Fail Threshold?

**Problem:** The false-negative deployment chain requires a 'decision-to-deploy threshold' to convert a continuous safety score into a pass/fail decision. No published research has applied formal standard-setting methodology (from educational testing) to AI safety evaluation. Current thresholds appear to be set ad hoc, creating arbitrary and inconsistent deployment decisions across labs and evaluators.

**Direction:** Apply two established standard-setting methods to an existing AI safety benchmark. Method 1 (Modified Angoff): Recruit 6-8 AI safety experts as panelists.
